prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. Starting in 1920, her reviews of comedies, tragedies, and musicals alike ended with a sentence about what standing room cost the city's clerks and shopgirls. A later index of her columns finds that sentence in all but a handful of the reviews she wrote over the next eleven years. Theater managers' letters from 1931 name her column when the three largest theaters halved standing-room prices, and the closing sentences stopped the following week. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: She closed nearly every review for eleven years with the same point about standing-room prices, and stopped only once the theaters cut them, so she was "insistent." "Mercurial" fails because she held to one point in all but a handful of reviews; "jaded" fails because she kept the campaign going season after season rather than growing weary; "judicious" fails because the closing sentence appeared whatever the play, so the passage shows persistence, not careful weighing of plays.

mercurial.quote: in all but a handful of the reviews
mercurial.why: returning to one point in nearly every review for years is the reverse of changeable

jaded.why: keeping up a campaign for over a decade shows energy, not weariness

judicious.why: the sentence ended her reviews regardless of the play, so it shows persistence about prices, not discernment about plays

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. In her last decade, she wrote that almost every new play reminded her of one she had already seen, and her reviews shrank to a paragraph that praised only the rare play she called unlike anything before it. Several plays she dismissed as familiar were praised by younger critics that same season and ran for years. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: After decades of reviewing, she found nearly every play a repeat and her reviews dwindled, so she had become "jaded." "Judicious" fails because the plays she dismissed as familiar were praised by others and ran for years, so her verdicts did not show sound judgment; "mercurial" fails because her dismissals were steady, not changeable; "insistent" fails because she was pressing no demand, only losing interest.

judicious.why: plays she waved off as familiar succeeded, so her verdicts reflect weariness, not good judgment

mercurial.quote: almost every new play reminded her
mercurial.why: her response was the same to nearly every play, which is consistency, not changeability

insistent.why: her reviews dwindled; she was withdrawing effort, not pressing a point

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. Her reviews weighed each play's strengths against its faults, and she rarely called a play either a masterpiece or a disaster. When a later scholar compared her verdicts with what became of the plays over the following fifty years, the plays she had praised were largely the ones still being staged, and those she had faulted had mostly been forgotten. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: She weighed merits against faults, avoided extremes, and her verdicts held up for fifty years, so she was "judicious." "Jaded" fails because she continued to find plays worth praising; "mercurial" fails because her verdicts were measured and borne out over time rather than swinging; "insistent" fails because nothing shows her pressing any demand.

jaded.why: she praised plays throughout, so she had not grown weary of the stage

mercurial.quote: rarely called a play either a masterpiece or a disaster
mercurial.why: she avoided extremes, the opposite of swinging between them

insistent.quote: weighed each play's strengths against its faults
insistent.why: her reviews balanced considerations; nothing is pressed again and again

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. In one season she called a play the finest of the year in March and, after seeing it again, tedious in April. The stage manager's logs show that the cast, the staging, and even the running time were unchanged between her two visits, and a later scholar found her reviews in other seasons reversing themselves about as often. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: She reversed her verdicts on unchanged plays, and did so often, so she was "mercurial." "Jaded" fails because she was capable of calling a play the finest of the year; "judicious" fails because verdicts that flip while the play stays the same do not reflect careful judgment; "insistent" fails because she held no position steadily.

jaded.why: a critic who can call a play the year's best has not grown weary of the stage

judicious.quote: were unchanged between her two visits
judicious.why: her verdict changed though the play did not, so the change came from her, not from careful weighing of the play

insistent.why: she kept changing positions rather than pressing one
